verses.text: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built Yahweh’s house and his own house,
Solomon built the cities which Huram had given to Solomon, and caused the children of Israel to dwell there.
Solomon went to Hamath Zobah, and prevailed against it.
He built Tadmor in the wilderness, and all the storage cities, which he built in Hamath.
Also he built Beth Horon the upper and Beth Horon the lower, fortified cities, with walls, gates, and bars;

and Baalath, and all the storage cities that Solomon had, and all the cities for his chariots, the cities for his horsemen, and all that Solomon desired to build for his pleasure in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
As for all the people who were left of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of Israel;
of their children who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel didn’t consume, of them Solomon conscripted forced labor to this day.
But of the children of Israel, Solomon made no servants for his work; but they were men of war, and chief of his captains, and rulers of his chariots and of his horsemen.
These were the chief officers of king Solomon, even two-hundred fifty, who ruled over the people.

Solomon brought up Pharaoh’s daughter out of David’s city to the house that he had built for her; for he said, “My wife shall not dwell in the house of David king of Israel, because the places where Yahweh’s ark has come are holy.”
Then Solomon offered burnt offerings to Yahweh on Yahweh’s altar, which he had built before the porch,

even as the duty of every day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and on the set feasts, three times per year, during the feast of unleavened bread, during the feast of weeks, and during the feast of tents.

He appointed, according to the ordinance of David his father, the divisions of the priests to their service, and the Levites to their offices, to praise and to minister before the priests, as the duty of every day required; the doorkeepers also by their divisions at every gate, for David the man of God had so commanded.
They didn’t depart from the commandment of the king to the priests and Levites concerning any matter, or concerning the treasures.
Now all the work of Solomon was prepared from the day of the foundation of Yahweh’s house until it was finished. So Yahweh’s house was completed.
Then Solomon went to Ezion Geber and to Eloth, on the seashore in the land of Edom.

Huram sent him ships and servants who had knowledge of the sea by the hands of his servants; and they came with the servants of Solomon to Ophir, and brought from there four hundred fifty talents  of gold, and brought them to king Solomon.

footnotes.content: Twenty years—what a long obedience in the same direction. Solomon built the Lord's house first, then his own. Notice the order tells you something about a heart still turning toward God, even if wealth and power will later turn it away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huram gave Solomon cities, and Solomon filled them with his own people. This is how flourishing spreads—neighbors help, and you settle your families in new ground. But notice: they can be given freely, yet still require faith and work to inhabit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hamath Zobah lay north of Israel, a stronghold that needed confronting. Solomon went and prevailed—a king's duty was to secure the borders so his people could live in peace. The Lord granted him strength to do it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tadmor in the wilderness—imagine building a city where nothing was. This speaks to Solomon's ambition to shape the land itself, to create storage and wealth. It's not wrong to build, but watch how this appetite will grow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beth Horon the upper and lower—these towns sat on a main road between the coast and Judah's heart. Fortified with walls and gates, they became a buffer, a stronghold. Solomon inherited a kingdom and strengthened what David had begun.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All that Solomon desired to build for his pleasure—those words carry a whisper of warning, don't they? Building cities for chariots and horses, for his own desire. A wise builder builds first for God and his people; a man of pleasure builds for himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites—all the peoples who remained after the conquest. They didn't vanish; they lived among Israel. Every kingdom carries within it peoples who arrived before us or came after. How we treat them speaks volumes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forced labor from the nations—Solomon used what remained of these peoples to build his projects. It's not chattel slavery, yet it's not freedom either. A lord's power often means others carry his dreams on their backs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the children of Israel he made no servants—they were men of war, captains, rulers. Solomon kept his own people free and gave them leadership. There's a kindness here, even if it's rooted in practicality: preserve your own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two hundred fifty chief officers—an enormous bureaucracy to rule the people and manage all those building projects. More men managing means fewer men free. Power requires machinery, and machinery consumes the free.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's daughter couldn't live in David's city because the ark had been there. Even in romance and politics, Solomon keeps one boundary sacred—the Lord's presence matters more than comfort. He separates the holy from the everyday, and that's wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon offered burnt offerings to the Lord on His altar—this is the turn toward home, toward gratitude. After all the building and rule-making, the king goes to the altar. The altar is the center, the steady point.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every day's duty, the Sabbaths, new moons, and set feasts—Solomon upheld the rhythm of worship that Moses ordained. Three times a year the nation gathered to remember. Rhythm keeps a heart turned toward the Lord when brilliance might otherwise turn it aside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's ordinance, kept by priests and Levites—Solomon inherited not just a kingdom but a priesthood. He appointed them as his father commanded, honoring the structure God had given. Humility is knowing you didn't invent wisdom; you steward it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They didn't depart from the king's commandment concerning treasures or service—obedience flowed downward through ranks. When a king honors the Lord's structure, those under him know what they're serving. Clear order can reflect clear devotion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From foundation to completion—the Lord's house was finished. Twenty years of labor, planning, sacrifice. A building stands as a witness, but only if the hearts that made it remain faithful. The building is done; the faithfulness is just beginning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ezion Geber and Eloth on the seashore—both ports in Edom, southern gateways to trade routes. Solomon reached to the sea itself. A kingdom expands, and a king's eyes stretch toward the horizon. Reach too far, though, and you lose the center.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huram sent ships with men who knew the sea, and they brought back gold—four hundred fifty talents. Readers today hear an echo of how the Lord provides through partnership and skill, how wealth flows when a king builds what's true. But they also see how abundance can seduce a good man into forgetting his source.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
